cards.title: Triple Close: Three Cart-Close Emails in One Day
cards.summary: Send three short cart-closing emails across morning, afternoon and evening of the final day instead of one or two.
cards.use_when: Planning the final day of a launch or sale campaign (cart close, promotion deadline, drop ending) and deciding how many closing emails to schedule.
steps: Schedule three closing emails on the final day: one in the morning, one in the afternoon, one in the evening. The source's client debated morning+afternoon vs afternoon+evening; the resolution was to send all three.
Vary subject lines rather than repeating the same one — casual late-night lines like 'you up?' were used for the last send.
Keep each closing email short and text-only; the goal is a reminder to act before the deadline, not new persuasion.

Attribute the reported results to this source's experience: triple close reportedly doubled total launch revenue in one case, and adding the third email alone added roughly 15–25% of total launch revenue. Treat these as examples, not promised benchmarks.
Test it yourself against your previous single- or double-close baseline before assuming the same lift for your list.
caveats: The revenue claims come from the presenter's own launches and one client; do not treat 15–25% as a guaranteed lift.
Three sends in one day raises unsubscribes and spam complaints on less engaged lists — segment to recent openers/clickers where possible.

cards.title: Late-Night Subject Lines: Short, Lowercase, No Punctuation
cards.summary: Use very short, casual, lowercase subject lines for late-evening sends and avoid periods that signal 'stop reading'.
cards.use_when: Writing subject lines for evening or final-day emails in a launch, flash sale or abandoned-cart sequence.
steps: Write the subject line as a casual check-in: 'you up', 'you're still up', 'just checking in'. The presenter takes the cue from the widely cited 'Hello' subject line attributed to Obama's campaign email.
Use lowercase and skip punctuation; a period reads as a full stop and invites deletion. Exclamation points are described as tolerable.
Reserve your grammatically careful subject lines for other emails — deliberately break the rule for late-night sends.
The presenter reports roughly a 32% open rate on a 600k-contact list with these lines, noting that open rates normally fall as list size grows. Verify against your own list before adopting at scale.
Write the subject line last, after drafting the body from an email outline, so it matches the content.
caveats: The 32% figure is one list's result, not a benchmark; large-list open rates vary by sender reputation and segmentation.
Lowercase, informal lines may underperform for premium or B2B ecommerce audiences — test before rolling out.

cards.title: Text-Only Emails to Stay Out of Promotions and Spam
cards.summary: Send plain-text emails without HTML templates or heavy images so promotions copy doesn't get filtered or clipped.
cards.use_when: Setting up any ecommerce email sequence — welcome, launch, or replenishment — where deliverability to the primary inbox matters.
steps: Strip out fancy HTML templates from your ESP (Mailchimp, etc.). The presenter says 'throw them in the garbage' — templates push emails into the Promotions tab and spam.
Load all content as plain text; only include a picture when it carries the message (e.g. a book cover, or a video thumbnail with a superimposed play button hyperlinked to the video).
Keep total email size under roughly two megabytes; oversized emails get clipped by email clients, and images easily exceed that.
Give up ornate formatting so the effort you put into writing isn't wasted in spam folders.
Keep the copy tight — the source says you don't need 'sat words' or showy vocabulary.
caveats: The 2MB clipping threshold is described approximately ('like two megabytes or something') — verify your ESP and client behavior.
Pure text reduces visual merchandising; if you rely heavily on product imagery, use linked video thumbnails or send traffic to a landing page instead.

cards.title: Write Email Sequences From an Outline Before Drafting
cards.summary: Decide the number of emails and their function first, then fill in subject, preview, story and content for each.
cards.use_when: Starting any ecommerce email campaign — launch, welcome, replenishment or abandoned-cart — and deciding where to begin.
steps: Commit to a quantity up front before writing anything. The source uses ten emails for a launch and seven for a welcome sequence as defaults; deviate only deliberately.
Build an outline row-by-row for each email: number it 1 through N, then for each write out subject, preview text, story, today's content and PS content.
Fill in the outline like kindergarten class — literally write email one, email two, email three, and so on.
Make sure the outline expresses the through-line of the whole sequence and what each email contributes to the broader objective.
Start writing as soon as possible after the outline so you're not staring at a blank page unprepared.
caveats: The 10-for-launch and 7-for-welcome numbers are the presenter's defaults, described as classic standards, not universal requirements.
A too-short or too-long sequence may not fit your catalog or list — the point is deciding the count on purpose.

cards.title: Seven-Email Welcome Series for New Subscribers
cards.summary: Send a daily seven-day welcome automation that delivers a video lesson and a short pitch while engagement is highest.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ecommerce welcome automation for new email signups, especially for a product that benefits from tutorials.
steps: Send an email per day for seven days as an automation; you don't need to obsess over unopens — it's automated, not a campaign.
For each day, link a video from your YouTube channel: hyperlink a video thumbnail with a superimposed play button, and under it, describe what the viewer will learn.
Include a call to action like 'if you want to check it out, click here', plus a PS that names a benefit and links again.
Strike while the iron is hot — the moment people first join is the most engaged they'll ever be, so pack value into these first days.
Aim to build positive open behavior: frequent opens train the inbox to keep your emails in the primary tab rather than Promotions or spam.
caveats: The source speaks from the perspective of teaching and B2C ecommerce clients; a seven-day daily cadence may feel heavy for lower-velocity or replenishment-only stores.
The claim that opens train the inbox is a heuristic — inbox placement is a black box; verify with your own deliverability data.

cards.title: Ecommerce Welcome Email #1: Discount Plus a Three-Column Best-Seller Block
cards.summary: Open with a welcome discount and a simple three-column best-sellers grid, then follow with product-tutorial emails.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first email of an ecommerce welcome sequence for a product-led store.
steps: Subject/body: 'hey you're confirmed, welcome' — then give the discount. Name the audience something ('the squad', 'the crew', 'the family') and present a coupon like $10 off.
Below the coupon, add a simple three-column grid of best-selling products with title and image, and one link per column.
Use 'best-selling products' rather than 'our best-selling products' — the presenter keeps the phrasing modest and less self-referential.

Follow with six more welcome emails, each demonstrating a product through a tutorial — e.g. 'how to curl a pixie cut' or 'how to straighten very curly hair without frizz' — linking to a video that demonstrates the product.
Rinse and repeat the tutorial-plus-link format for all remaining emails.
caveats: The reported figures — $75k/month from the first email and $145k/month from the full sequence for a hair-tool brand — are one client's results, not a forecast.
Tutorial-based welcome emails work well for demonstrable products; pure commodity items may need a different first-email hook.

cards.title: Match Sales-Page Copy to Customer Awareness Stage
cards.summary: Set story length and proof density based on how aware the buyer is of their problem, the solution category, and your product.
cards.use_when: Writing a product sales page, long-form landing page or launch email and deciding how much story to tell before selling.
steps: Classify the audience on the awareness scale, drawn from the car-buying example: unaware (doesn't know the problem), problem-aware (knows a problem exists, not the solution), solution-aware (knows solutions exist — bikes, buses, cars), product-aware (has decided to buy a category and is choosing), and most aware (knows exactly which one they want).
For unaware and problem-aware audiences, build up the problem first with a longer story — describe common failed attempts (e.g. keto, zumba, rebound weight) and explain why nothing worked.
For solution- and product-aware audiences, shorten the story and add more testimonials and comparisons between options.
For most-aware buyers (the 'I want a Mercedes' stage), cut your story and sell the product — the source says 'shut up about your story' and show them their options.
Match the source's default: if your audience sits between problem- and solution-aware (roughly stages 3–4), use a medium to long story.
caveats: The stage framework is a heuristic, not a formula; some audiences straddle levels, and product-aware buyers still want price/availability clarity.
Awareness stages must be inferred from traffic source and customer research — don't assume your store's visitors are all the same stage.

cards.title: Sales-Page Template and Section Order
cards.summary: Copy a fixed section order — hero, story, proof, price positioning, objections, FAQs, repeated CTAs — to prevent incoherent pages.
cards.use_when: Building a sales page, product landing page or long-form collection page and deciding section-by-section structure.
steps: Write the hero section first: headline, sub-headline and a call to action. Don't name the product unless you're a household brand like mercedes.com or apple.com — a Mercedes-level brand can get away with it, a newer store cannot.
Write the story section at the length matching your audience's awareness stage.
Show why they need the product, then show what happens without it.
Insert testimonials and success stories, then position the price (offer stack or comparison).
Handle objections ('what if you took my money and I want it back?'), add FAQs, then more testimonials.
Slip in a call to action or pricing table every two or three content sections so the reader can buy at any point of readiness.
caveats: The source gives the template as a starting point and adapts it — don't treat section order as a rigid law.
The references to mercedes.com and apple.com are illustrative brand examples, not licensing to name-drop in your copy.

cards.title: Building a Cohesive Through-Line From Sub-Headers
cards.summary: Test sales-page cohesion by reading only the sub-headlines and checking whether they tell a complete story.
cards.use_when: Editing a sales page, landing page or launch sequence and deciding whether the sections connect.
steps: Isolate the sub-headlines and read them in sequence. Example from the source's purpose-course page: 'it's Monday morning, ugh'; 'it's Monday already, just five more minutes'; 'hey, at least it pays the bills'; 'we need a massive culture shift'.
If those lines don't tell a coherent story from problem to possibility, the page lacks a through-line and readers will drop off.
Rewrite sub-headlines to advance an argument in a logical order that matches how customers explain and feel about the problem.
Check the same coherence in your email sequence — each email's role in the arc should be visible from its outline position.
caveats: The 'number one problem' diagnosis is the presenter's opinion, not a measured finding.
This test works for long-form pages; short pages with one section rarely need a through-line.

cards.title: Sentiment Matching: Mine Reviews for Your Customer's Own Words
cards.summary: Read 5-star and 1-star reviews of competing or analogous products to learn the exact language customers use about the problem.
cards.use_when: Starting a product launch, PDP rewrite or ad campaign and needing customer language to write copy in.
steps: Read your own customer testimonials first if you have them.

If you don't, read reviews of competitors and analogous products: Amazon book, video or course reviews in the same category; if you're in relationships, look up another relationship coach with the same format.
Read both five-star reviews and one-star reviews — 5-star shows what people love, 1-star shows what they hate.
Use the findings to position the product: 'I'm not like the stuff you hate, but I am like the stuff you love'.
Note the exact words and phrases buyers use to describe their problem, and echo those words in the headline, story and object handling.
caveats: The source's example is a coaching business; the ecommerce translation is reading competitor product reviews to identify language — the demonstrated result was for non-ecommerce courses.
Amazon/course reviews may reflect different buyers than your store's audience; verify against your own customer support themes.

cards.title: Positioning the Price: Offer Stack or Apples-to-Oranges Comparison
cards.summary: Break your offer into individual features with value assigned, or compare your price against the cost of alternatives.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to present pricing on a sales page, bundle page or checkout for high-ticket or multi-part offers.
steps: Build an offer stack: list the individual features of the overall package and assign a value to each ('total X value, total investment starting at Y'). End with 'priceless' as the master-card-style kicker — the source uses this and reports it lands.
If itemizing features makes no sense for your offer, use an apples-to-oranges comparison instead.
Positive variant: show what it would cost for a trainer, a personal chef and a nutritionist making your menus — isn't it easier to pay $3.99 and get all of them?
Negative variant: show the cost of inaction — a heart attack is expensive, missing your daughter's wedding isn't worth skipping the payment.
Pick the variant that matches your audience's emotional driver; the source presents both as valid situational alternatives.
caveats: The 'total value' figures are marketing constructs — inflated itemized values can erode trust if the gap to price is absurd.
Negative fear-based framing can misfire with certain audiences and platforms; check ad policy and brand tone.

cards.title: Plan the Email Count Before You Write the Sequence
cards.summary: Decide the number of emails in a launch or welcome sequence up front, then fill in the outline.
cards.use_when: Starting a launch or welcome sequence and planning how many sends are needed.
steps: For a launch: default to ten emails unless you have a specific reason to deviate.
For a welcome sequence: default to seven emails.
State the target count out loud before writing so you know when the sequence is finished.
Work through the outline row-by-row (subject, preview, story, content, PS) — then start writing as soon as possible.
Map each email to a clear function in the broader objective so you know what each one is for.
caveats: These are the presenter's defaults, described as classic standards — not requirements for every catalog or audience.
Deviating is fine provided the deviation is deliberate, not accidental.

cards.title: Use Second-Person 'You' Copy and Drop Your Own Logic
cards.summary: Write in second person and reason with the customer's logic, not yours, since their background and framing differ from yours.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing email, PDP or ad copy where the copy favors the brand's reasoning over the buyer's.
steps: Audit drafts for first-person framing — 'we built', 'our process', 'our story' — and convert them to 'you' framing.
Avoid selling via your own logic chain; the customer arrives with a different set of experiences and their own narration of the problem.
Use sentiment matching (reviews, testimonials) to learn the customer's logic, then write to that logic.
Check each paragraph: does it help the reader see their situation more clearly, or explain your reasoning?
caveats: Second person is a default, not a prohibition on first-person in testimonials, brand story pages or about-us content.
Sentiment matching takes research time; skipping it and defaulting to your own logic defeats the purpose.

cards.title: Choosing Email Software: Mailchimp, ActiveCampaign, or Infusionsoft
cards.summary: Pick beginner, intermediate or enterprise email software based on list size and membership-site needs.
cards.use_when: Selecting an ESP for a growing ecommerce store and deciding when to migrate.
steps: If you're just starting and list size is small, Mailchimp is the source's recommendation — the presenter has worked with clients up to 165,000 contacts on it, though they moved those clients off once it got large.
At a few thousand subscribers, ActiveCampaign is described as a good intermediate step.
If you don't need Infusionsoft, the source says don't use it.

Infusionsoft is only justified in two cases per the source: (1) huge lists of roughly 600,000 to 1,000,000+ contacts, or (2) membership sites, where it integrates better with membership-site software than competing ESPs. The source says membership-site use justifies it at around 1,000+ members.
Otherwise, choose the lower-complexity tool and migrate up only when a trigger threshold is hit.
caveats: Tooling capability and pricing change frequently — verify current interfaces and plans before committing.
The list-size thresholds are the presenter's heuristics, not vendor limits; your own engagement and segmentation needs may force migration sooner.

cards.title: Use Short Headlines to Carry a Story Across a Page
cards.summary: Write sales-page headlines that function as a sequence of mini-lines telling the reader's story in order.
cards.use_when: Writing the hero section and section headers of a product or launch sales page.
steps: Write consecutive short lines that build a narrative arc — the source's example: 'you're starting an exciting journey'; 'Hollywood doesn't make it easy'; 'if you're serious about your craft'.
Tie each line to a customer-voiced belief rather than a brand claim: actors believe Hollywood is institutionally harder than it should be, and the copy validates that belief before selling.
Name the exact thing the audience already agrees on — actors constantly take classes, read trade magazines, attend casting workshops — so the copy speaks in-language.
Keep sections short enough that a reader skimming only headlines still gets the argument.
Make the last section a positioning and price section rather than another story beat.
caveats: The examples are drawn from coaching and acting courses, not ecommerce — transfer the structure of customer-voiced headline sequences, not the specific lines.
Story-heavy headlines can slow a product page for bottom-of-funnel traffic; consider testing short benefit headers there.

cards.title: Punctuation and Formatting Discipline in Subject Lines
cards.summary: Avoid punctuation that signals stopping and reserve periods for body copy, not the subject line.
cards.use_when: Reviewing subject lines in any ecommerce email campaign before launch.
steps: Do not use periods in subject lines — the source says a period means 'stop reading' and invites deletion.
Exclamation points are described as tolerable; keep everything else minimal.
Skip elaborate vocabulary and decorative phrasing; plain, spoken language outperforms ornate prose in the source's experience.
Apply these rules across the whole sequence, reserving grammatically careful lines for the body where tone matters more than open behavior.
caveats: These are the presenter's stated preferences from their own sending practice, not empirical standards; brand voice in some categories tolerates punctuation.
Test punctuation choices against your own open rates before treating them as rules.

cards.title: Start Writing Copy as Soon as Possible, Even by Hand
cards.summary: Get a first draft down quickly to avoid blank-page paralysis — outline first, then write fast.
cards.use_when: Failing to start a launch, welcome or PDP copy project because the scope feels overwhelming.
steps: Decide the email count or page sections in outline form before writing words (ten for launch, seven for welcome as defaults).
Write a full, rough line for each outline cell — subject, preview, story, content, PS — then start writing immediately.
Accept that the draft doesn't need to be clever; the outline does the thinking.
Don't freeze trying to pick perfect words; send the first draft into revision.
Use the same approach on a sales page: decide the story length first, then write the hero and build down.
caveats: Speed drafting works only after the outline phase — writing blind just produces incoherent copy faster.
The source's preference for committing quickly is a practice suggestion, not a quality guarantee.
